Nanobubble water promotes anaerobic digestion of high-solids cattle 
manure under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions 
Qingfang Zhang a, Ruoyu Wu a, Ziying Xu a, Yutong Feng a, Cheng Peng a, Hailong Shi a, 
Yuqian Zhang a, Linhai Yang a, Dan Luo a, Peng Dong a, Wenqi Gao b, Tianfeng Wang a,*

b School of Civil Engineering, Lanzhou Institute of Technology, Lanzhou, 730050, China   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords:

Microbial community 
Correlation 
A B S T R A C T   
The gradual increase in cattle farming has led to a huge production of cattle manure (CM), but the conventional 
treatment methods are less efficient. In this study, the treatment method of anaerobic digestion (AD) of high- 
solids CM by combining nanobubble water (NBW) with different gases was proposed to present a new idea 
for the reduction, harmlessness, and resourcefulness of CM. It was found that the performance of the digester 
with added NBW was better than the control. Among them, the cumulative methane yield T-Air: 227.09 mL g−1 
VSadded and T-CO2: 226.12 mL g−1 VSadded increased by 17.72 % and 17.22 %, respectively, compared with the 
control T: 192.90 mL g−1 VSadded under thermophilic conditions. Under mesophilic conditions, M-Air: 162.39 
mL g−1 VSadded increased by 9.68 % compared with control M: 148.05 mL g−1 VSadded. Microbial communities 
analyzed at the genus level revealed that the relative abundance of bacteria favorable to hydrolysis and acid- 
producing processes, such as Defluviitalea, Haloplasma, and Bacillus, increased to varying degrees. Moreover, 
the relative abundance of archaea favorable for methanogenesis, such as Methanoculleus, Methanobrevibacter, and 
Methanosarcina, also increased to varying degrees. Therefore, the addition of NBW promoted the hydrolysis of 
high-solids CM, enhanced the stability of the reaction, improved the methanogenic performance, and increased 
the RA of favorable genera, which ultimately led to a better performance of the AD of high-solids CM.   
1. Introduction 
Livestock is an important contributor to the global agricultural 
market, and to meet the growing demand for meat, traditional decen­
tralized family-scale livestock farms are gradually being transformed 
into centralized livestock farms. As a result, these farms are faced with 
being "flooded" with large quantities of manure that are constantly being 
produced (Li et al., 2021). Major cattle-producing countries include the 
United States, which has over 94 million head, the United Kingdom, 
which raises tens of millions of cows and calves annually, as well as 
other countries such as Brazil, with 218 million head, India, with 186 
million head, Argentina, with 53 million head, and Australia, with 26 
million head (Font-Palma, 2019). This situation is also adapted to China, 
in which in 2023 about 102 million head of cattle will be raised in the 
country (MAFF, 2023). It is estimated that one cow produces about 10 kg 
of cow manure (CM) per day (Tariq et al., 2022), so China produces 
about 1 billion tons of CM per day. If this CM is not managed effectively, 
various problems will occur, such as air pollution, water pollution, the 
proliferation of harmful bacteria, and the release of toxic substances 
(Zeng et al., 2024). Currently, the main solution is to use most of the CM 
as fertilizer on agricultural land to improve soil fertility and crop yield 
(Yan et al., 2022). However, to some extent, the long-term utilization of 
this method leads to the increasing accumulation of some heavy metals 
(e.g., cadmium and mercury) in agricultural soils (Liu et al., 2020). So 
improper treatment of CM may give significant health risks and envi­
ronmental problems. Therefore, it is crucial to utilize appropriate 
methods to treat CM in a harmless, reduced, and resourceful way. 
As to manure treatment, anaerobic digestion (AD) is a suitable 
method, as this method can simultaneously degrade organic matter, 
harmlessly discard wastes, and generate clean energy through a series of 
biological processes (Mumtaz et al., 2023; Neshat et al., 2017). Among 
them, high solid anaerobic digestion (HSAD) (usually referred to as 
digestate TS content higher than 8%) is an outstanding technology for 
harvesting energy from organic waste (Fan et al., 2020). This technology

achieves a lower moisture content in the digestive system, lower 
wastewater production, lower digester volume, higher volumetric 
methane yield rate, and digestates with higher fertilizer potential (Bao 
et al., 2023). 
The HSAD process is highly influenced by the composition of the 
manure, which, depending on the source, may contain a high load of 
recalcitrant substances or lead to the formation of toxic compounds (e. 
g., NH3), which results in a slow and incomplete hydrolysis phase, a 
decrease in the cumulative methane yield (CMY), and, ultimately, a 
decrease in the energy potential of the waste (Anacleto et al., 2022). For 
example, CM contains a large amount of lignocellulose, and these 
recalcitrant parts may hinder the hydrolysis of CM in AD due to its 
complex structure, coupled with the fact that HSAD itself is more diffi­
cult to hydrolyze, so the use of CM as a substrate will severely limit the 
rate and effect of hydrolysis, resulting in a reactor that is susceptible to 
inhibition and longer lag periods, which will ultimately affect the yield 
and rate of methane (Neshat et al., 2017). 
Besides, temperature is an important factor in HSAD, and HSAD 
exhibits different characteristics under mesophilic and thermophilic 
operating conditions. Mesophilic HSAD (25 ◦C–40 ◦C) has been widely 
used because of its good stability (Wang et al., 2023). Thermophilic 
HSAD (>45 ◦C), on the one hand, is limited in its application due to its 
high energy demand and poor stability. On the other hand, it is favored 
for its higher hydrolysis rate, fast gas production rate, and high methane 
production potential (Liu et al., 2022). Anaerobic co-digestion and 
Pretreatment (e.g., thermal pretreatments, physical pretreatments, and 
chemical pretreatments) (Anacleto et al., 2022; Di Capua et al., 2020; 
Venkateshkumar et al., 2023), are often used to improve HSAD perfor­
mance. However, most of these pretreatment methods have not been 
applied in industries due to chemical contamination, high energy con­
sumption, low post-waste utilization, or operational complexity (Wang 
et al., 2020). Simple and cost-effective methods are needed to improve 
CM difficult hydrolysis and digester stability during HSAD while 
improving methane productivity. 
Nanobubble water (NBW) is a body of water that contains a large 
number of nanoscale particulate bubbles (Atkinson et al., 2019). It 
possesses properties not found in ordinary water, such as the ability to 
generate reactive oxygen species (e.g., O2⋅-, H2O, 1O2, or ⋅OH), high 
negative ζ-potential, low buoyancy, high gas solubility, long residence 
time, and high surface charge. Whereas, water plays a crucial role in the 
anaerobic digestion process by promoting substrate hydrolysis and 
transferring hydrolysis products and other intermediates to places 
where they can be utilized by microorganisms (Kothari et al., 2014). 
Therefore, the concept of coupling NBW with AD is feasible. Moreover, 
the preparation method of NBW is simple and inexpensive, which only 
requires an instrument to pump gas into tap water or distilled water, 
which can produce 8–11 L of NBW per minute (Wang et al., 2019), and 
more critically, the process of NBW generation and application are both 
green (Chuenchart et al., 2021). So, this technology has the potential to 
be applied in practical engineering. 
Different gases can produce different types of NBW, such as Air, CO2, 
H2, N2, or O2, which produce NBW that can be used in different digestion 
substrates. A study found that the addition of air-nanobubble water (Air- 
NBW) increased total alkalinity (TA) and partial alkalinity (PA) and 
decreased the volatile fatty acid (VFAs)/TA ratio; as a result, the stability 
of the AD process was maintained (Fan et al., 2021a). Nanobubbles 
increased water mobility and resulted in the higher mass transfer of 
nutrients to the microbial cells, which increased enzyme activity and 
decomposition rates for substrates with more CMY (Wang et al., 2019). 
The addition of N2 and Air-NBW to the AD system of kitchen waste found 
that the activity of hydrolytic enzymes increased by 8 %–47 % in the first 
phase, and the activity of coenzyme F420 increased significantly by 34 % 
in the second phase (Hou et al., 2021b). The results indicated that the 
CMY of the digester with NBW addition of pig manure was 19 %–39 % 
higher than that of the control group (without NBW addition) (Fan et al., 
2021b). 
In summary, conventional processes for the treatment of high 
organic content wastes may result in disadvantages such as slow and 
incomplete substrate hydrolysis stages, unstable reaction systems, and 
lower cumulative methane production, ultimately resulting in lower 
energy potential of the waste. However, the unique characteristics of 
NBW may improve the above disadvantages. The NBW coupled HSAD 
process is easy to operate without adding too many chemicals and is 
environmentally friendly, making NBW an innovative alternative to 
reduce the use of chemicals and energy. However, so far, the application 
of NBW in HSAD has been reported less, and most of the studies on the 
application of NBW in HSAD were carried out under mesophilic condi­
tions, and the performance changes of NBW on HSAD under thermo­
philic conditions are not clear. And this study reveals for the first time 
the effects of different NBW on the performance of HSAD reaction with 
CM as substrate under thermophilic and mesophilic conditions. So it is 
still unknown whether NBW can effectively improve the performance of 
HSAD with CM as a substrate. By exploring the mechanisms related to 
the changes in hydrolysis rate, stability, methane yield, and other 
properties of NBW-HSAD at different temperatures and different NBW, 
and the changes in the microbial community structure, new insights into 
the digestion process were improved. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Materials 
Fresh CM was obtained from Holstein cows. Before the experiment, 
the CM was stored in the refrigerator at 4 ± 1 ◦C. Waste-activated sludge 
was domesticated under thermophilic (55 ± 1 ◦C) and mesophilic (37 ±
1 ◦C) conditions after retrieval and then used as inoculated sludge. The 
physicochemical characteristics of CM and inoculum are shown in 
Table 1. 
2.2. Preparation of NBW 
NBW was produced by a nanobubble generator (JWNP, AL01S, 
China) through which Air, CO2, He, and N2 were introduced at 20 ±
2 ◦C. The deionized water (DW) in the vessel was recirculated into the 
generator recirculation system for 20 min to obtain the requisite NBW. 
Freshly prepared NBW is a white opaque liquid that then becomes 
colorless and transparent after 5–10 min of standing. This phenomenon 
occurs because many visible microscopic bubbles rise to the surface, 
rupture, and disappear. The pressure was controlled at 0.4–0.5 MPa 
during the production of NBW. 
2.3. Experimental setup 
The experimental setup was similar to that in our previous study (Liu 
et al., 2022). The mass of substrate in each digester was 818 g (CM: 
NBW = 1:1, TS was approximately 13 %), and 82 g of inoculated sludge

thermophilic and mesophilic conditions. DW (T and M) was used as the 
control group, and different NBW, including Air-NBW, carbon 
dioxide-nanobubble water (CO2-NBW), helium-nanobubble water 
(He-NBW), and nitrogen-nanobubble water (N2-NBW), were used as the 
experimental group. The different NBW were identified as M, M-Air, 
M-CO2, M-He, and M-N2 under mesophilic conditions and as T, T-Air, 
T-CO2, T-He, and T-N2 under thermophilic conditions. Each working 
condition was carried out in triplicate, and no pH adjustment was per­
formed in this study to prevent microenvironmental variations and 
simplify this HSAD process, which might be applied in practice. The 
thermophilic digesters and the mesophilic digesters were heated in a 
water bath at 55 ± 1 ◦C and 37 ± 1 ◦C. Finally, each digester was shaken 
for 1 min at a fixed time each day. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
The TA, TS, pH, VS, soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), and 
total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) of the samples were determined using 
standard methods (APHA, 1998). The determination of free ammonia 
nitrogen (FAN) in liquid samples was carried out using the formula 
provided by (Hansen et al., 1998). The VFAs content was determined 
using a gas chromatograph with a flame ionization detector (SP-7890 
Plus, Ruihong, China). The volume and composition of biogas were 
determined by a gas flow meter (LML-2, Alpha, China) and a biogas 
analyzer (GA 5000, Geotach, United Kingdom), respectively. The C, H, 
N, and S content of the samples was determined using an organic 
elemental analyzer (Vario EL Cube, Elementar, Deutschland). 
The HiPure Soil DNA kit (Magen, Guangzhou, China) was used for 
digestate deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) extraction following the HSAD 
process. Microbial communities were analyzed by sequencing the highly 
variable V3–V4 and V4–V5 regions of the 16S rDNA gene. Bacteria were 
amplified with primers 341 F (5′CCTACGGGGNGGCWGCAG-3′) and 
806 R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTATCTAAT-3′), and archaea were amplified 
with primers Arch 519 F (5′-CAGCMGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and Arch 915 R 
(5′- GTGCTCCCCCGCCAATTCCT-3′) amplification. The amplified prod­
ucts obtained from PCR were recovered cut, and quantified using a 
QuantiFluorTM fluorometer. The purified amplification products were 
then mixed in equal amounts and connected to sequencing connectors. 
Subsequently, sequencing libraries were constructed, and Illumina 
PE250 was used for up-sequencing. Finally, the raw data obtained from 
microbial sequencing were uploaded to the website (https://www.ncbi. 
nlm.nih.gov) under the bacterial accession number PRJNA1060892, and 
the archaeal accession number PRJNA1060904. 
2.5. Statistical analysis 
The correlations were statistically analyzed using SPSS software 
version 27.0 for Windows. Correlation analysis was performed for the 
process parameters, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically signifi­
cant. Analyses were performed based on Pearson’s rank correlation, * 
representing P < 0.05, ** representing P < 0.01 (the smaller the P-value, 
the better the correlation). Orange and red show a positive correlation, 
light blue and dark blue show a negative correlation, and the darker the 
color is the greater the correlation. AD experiments and NBW charac­
terization tests were performed using Microsoft Office Excel 2019 to 
calculate the mean value ± standard deviation of three parallel experi­
ments. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post 
hoc test was performed to evaluate the significant differences regarding 
performance indicators. The analysis of methane yield was fitted to the 
methane yield by a modified Gompertz model as our previous study (Liu 
et al., 2022). 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Changes in digestate characteristics 
3.1.1. VFAs 
VFAs are a product of hydrolysis and acidification and are a substrate 
used to obtain methane (Chen et al., 2022). The trend of VFAs in the 
thermophilic digester was similar to that of SCOD in that it increased 
first and then decreased (Fig. 1, Fig. 3a). VFAs in all digesters at ther­
mophilic peaked on the fifth day. The concentration of VFAs was higher 
in the digesters with NBW added compared with T. The concentration of 
VFAs in T-Air was the highest and decreased fast. This suggests that the 
addition of Air-NBW may lead to more efficient hydrolysis, more com­
plete substrate degradation, and faster conversion of VFAs to methane in 
the reaction, which is in line with the results of the subsequent study 
(Fig. 4 and Table 2). The concentration of VFAs in T-He was high but 
decreased slowly. The high VFAs concentration of T-CO2, but the sub­
sequent methane production was very good, suggesting that the VFAs 
concentration of T-CO2 may have peaked five days ago and declined 
rapidly. The concentration of VFAs was higher in the mesophilic digester 
compared with the thermophilic digester, but the decline was slower. 
This phenomenon may be related to the faster rate of methane pro­
duction under thermophilic conditions (Fig. 4 and Table 2). All of the 
mesophilic digesters, except M-Air, had peak VFAs concentrations on the 
fifth day. The lower VFAs concentration in M-Air compared with M may 
be due to its higher VFAs production/conversion efficiency. However, 
the VFAs concentration of CM under mesophilic conditions in this study 
was lower than that of Fan et al. (2020) using pig manure as a substrate. 
This is supposedly because the lignocellulose contained in CM is difficult 
to degrade (Haque et al., 2022). 
3.1.2. pH, TA and TVFAs/TA 
The pH (Fig. 2a and b) of digestate is mainly influenced by the bal­
ance between ammonia and VFAs, which depends on the balance be­
tween hydrolysis, acid production (acetic acid production), and 
methane yield (Bai et al., 2015). During the HSAD process, the small 
difference in pH between the control and experimental groups occurs 
because the digestion substrate ratios are identical and the CM mecha­
nism is relatively stable, resulting in little fluctuation in pH. The pH of 
thermophilic digesters is higher than that of mesophilic digesters. 
Because the rate of hydrolysis and acidification of proteins are faster 
under thermophilic conditions, a large amount of organic nitrogen is 
converted to ammonia nitrogen, and VFAs accumulates rapidly but is 
degraded rapidly; thus, the pH value is generally higher than that under 
mesophilic conditions due to the high ammonia nitrogen under ther­
mophilic conditions and the rapid degradation of VFAs (Li et al., 2023). 
The pH of the digesters (Fig. 2a) stabilized between 8.06–8.45 under 
thermophilic conditions and between 7.55–8.00 under mesophilic con­
ditions (Fig. 2b). This is the pH range acceptable for metabolism by 
methanogens and related bacteria, and the HSAD system is relatively 
stable (Li et al., 2017). 
TA is tied to the buffering capacity of the digester (Kawasaki et al., 
2020). Under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions, so the TA of the 
digesters were all increased and then stabilized (Fig. 2c and d), which 
may be due to the fact that the CM in the digested substrate contains a 
large amount of alkali metals (Ca and Mg), which contributes to the 
alkalinity (Li et al., 2021). However, the TA contents of all samples, 
including those with the addition of NBW, were slightly higher than 
those with the addition of DW. This suggests that the addition of NBW 
may increase the TA content when the HSAD system is slightly inhibited, 
which is favorable for the recovery of the stability of the HSAD system. 
TVFAs/TA is a good indicator of digester stability (Fan et al., 2020). 
When TVFAs/TA < 0.35, TA is sufficient to buffer TVFAs, and the AD 
digester can operate stably; when TVFAs/TA > 0.8, the AD digester 
operation is extremely unstable (Liu et al., 2022). At the beginning of the 
experiment, the TVFAs/TA of the thermophilic digester reached

TVFAs/TA of all digesters gradually decreased to below 0.35 as the 
HSAD reaction proceeded, which indicated that the HSAD process was 
stabilizing. 
3.1.3. SCOD, TAN, and FAN 
SCOD refers to soluble chemical oxygen demand, an important in­
dicator of the anaerobic digestion process; the SCOD indicates the 
amount of soluble organic matter in the digestate (Poorasgari and 
¨Ormeci, 2022). Therefore, the hydrolytic acidification during the HSAD 
reaction of CM can be expressed as SCOD. The SCOD for all digesters 
reached their respective maximum values and then began to decline 
(Fig. 3a and b), because the conversion of substrate to soluble organic 
matter during hydrolysis increased SCOD in the first stage, and then 
with the consumption of organic acids by methanogen, SCOD was 
partially removed through biogas formation to decrease SCOD, so the 
differences in SCOD values were also closely related to gas production 
(Vu and Min, 2019). In particular, the SCOD in T-Air reached 24163.66 
mg L−1 in the thermophilic digester on the fifth day, which was 33.4 % 
higher than that in T and decreased rapidly (Fig. 3a). Suggesting that the 
addition of Air-NBW may have promoted the hydrolysis of substrates in 
the HSAD hydrolysis and acidification stages. Although conducted under 
anaerobic conditions, the addition of Air did not stop the HSAD reaction, 
probably because the environment rapidly becomes anaerobic when the 
presence of limited trace oxygen can be rapidly consumed by aerobic or 
parthenogenetic anaerobic bacteria, which is similar to the results of the 
previous research (Xu et al., 2018). The smallest SCOD of T-CO2 was 
found to be 16978.49 mg L−1, but its gas production was very good, 
which indicated that the addition of CO2-NBW led to faster HSAD

Ammonia is a byproduct of the hydrolysis of proteinaceous material 
(Sung and Liu, 2003). Utilizing an appropriate concentration of total 
ammonia nitrogen is beneficial to biological growth, as ammonia ni­
trogen provides a buffer and nutrients for microbial growth; however, 
when the ammonia concentration exceeds 1500 mg L−1 it will inhibit AD 
hydrolysis and acid production, and the activity of methanogens will be 
affected, which will ultimately lead to a decrease in CH4 production 
(Pavez-Jara et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021). During HSAD, the TAN 
concentration in all digesters gradually increased and then stabilized 
(Fig. 3c and d). This may have increased the inorganic nitrogen content 
including ammonia nitrogen by decomposition of soluble organic 
nitrogen such as protein in the HSAD reaction. The concentration of TAN 
in each of these digesters was generally around 1500 mg L−1, which 
indicates that most of the digesters were not significantly affected by 
ammonia. In addition, the ammonia nitrogen concentrations of T and M 
were generally lower than those of the experimental group with the 
addition of NBW, suggesting that the addition of NBW may have 
improved the hydrolysis effect, resulting in a more complete hydrolysis 
of the substrate leading to generally higher ammonia nitrogen concen­
trations. However, TAN is less toxic than FAN because FAN is able to 
penetrate the cell membrane of microorganisms and accumulate inside 
the cell, causing a proton imbalance or toxic cytoplasmic enzymes (Su 
et al., 2023). So excess FAN is a key toxicant for methanogenic com­
munities during HSAD, and methanogens were largely inhibited at FAN 
concentrations above 250 mg L−1 (Sung and Liu, 2003). At the end of the 
HSAD reaction, the concentration of FAN in the thermophilic digester 
ranged from 353.04 to 419.48 mg L−1, both of which were greater than 
the FAN threshold (Fig. 3e), and the concentration of FAN in the mes­
ophilic digester ranged from 102.68 to 122.71 mg L−1, both less than the 
FAN threshold (Fig. 3f). Therefore, methanogen in the thermophilic 
digester may have been inhibited, and methanogen in the mesophilic

3.2. Methane yield 
Methane yield is often considered a crucial indicator for evaluating 
anaerobic digestion performance (Yao et al., 2017). The cumulative CH4 
yields under thermophilic conditions were as follows: T: 192.90 mL g−1 
VSadded, T-Air: 227.09 mL g−1 VSadded, T-CO2: 226.12 mL g−1 VSadded, 
T-He: 184.74 mL g−1 VSadded and T-N2:198.98 mL g−1 VSadded (Fig. 4a). 
Among them, T-Air and T-CO2 increased CMY by 17.72% and 17.22%, 
respectively, compared with T, and also produced methane at a signif­
icantly faster rate than T (Fig. 4c). Additionally, the mean CMY values of 
T-Air and T-CO2 differed significantly (P < 0.05) from T. The cumulative 
CH4 yields under mesophilic conditions as follows: M: 148.05 mL g−1 
VSadded, M-Air: 162.40 mL g−1 VSadded, M-CO2: 151.20 mL g−1 VSadded, 
M-He: 154.85 mL g−1 VSadded, and M-N2: 140.37 mL g−1 VSadded 
(Fig. 4b). Among them, M-Air showed a 9.68% increase in CMY 
compared with M and also had a significantly faster rate of methane 
production than M (Fig. 4d). Additionally, a significant difference (P <
0.05) was observed in the mean value of CMY between M-Air and M. The 
level of methane production is also related to the stability of the system,

3.3. Characteristics of the microbial community 
3.3.1. Dominant bacterial community 
In the HSAD system, bacteria play an important role in the hydrolysis 
and acidification phases, effectively degrading macromolecules into 
amino acids, sugars, and alcohols and converting these small molecules 
into VFAs (Yu et al., 2023). However, changes in the abundance of the 
bacterial communities in the HSAD system were different with 
increasing fermentation time. In order to elucidate microbial transitions 
in the HSAD system, bacterial sequences at the genus level and with 
relative abundance (RA) greater than 1 % were selected in this study to 
represent the changing signs of the bacterial community. 
The dominant genera under thermophilic conditions in the early 
stage of HSAD were Defluviitalea, Haloplasma, and Lysinibacillus, which 
accounted for 36.3 %–42.2 %, 3.4 %–6.9 %, and 0.03 %–6.8 % of the 
total sequences, respectively, with RA > 5.0% (Fig. 5a). Among them, 
Defluviitalea can be selectively enriched under thermophilic conditions 
and plays a role in the oxidation of intercalated acetates, degradation of 
intercalated alcohols and lactates, degradation of composite com­
pounds, and degradation of proteinaceous substances (Jiang et al., 
2020). However, the RA of Defluviitalea with the addition of NBW were 
all higher than that of T (RA = 36.3 %), and Defluviitalea was signifi­
cantly and positively correlated with CMY and the methane yield rate (P 
< 0.01) and significantly and negatively correlated with the lag period 
(P < 0.01) (Fig. 6). This suggests that NBW may have a facilitating effect 
on substrate degradation, causing the digester to increase the rate of 
methane production, shorten the lag period, and increase CMY. As the 
reaction proceeded, the RA of Defluviitalea decreased from 36.3 %–42.2 
%–0.7 % to 1.9 % (Fig. 5b), which suggests that the substrate in the 
digester was gradually being degraded, and the nutrient available for 
Defluviitalea to this indicates that the substrate in the digester was 
gradually degraded and the nutrients available for Defluviitalea to utilize 
were gradually reduced, resulting in a decrease in RA. Haloplasma is

3.3.2. Dominant archaeal community 
In HSAD, archaea are the most important microorganisms in the 
methane yield process, and they are distinguished from bacteria by 
unique ribosomal RNA, the absence of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, 
and different membrane lipids (Harirchi et al., 2022). However, changes 
in the abundance of archaeal communities in anaerobic fermentation 
systems varied with increasing fermentation time. The variation in the 
archaeal community at the genus level is shown in Figures, which can be 
used to elucidate the microbial transition in HSAD (Fig. 7a and b). 
The dominant genera in the archaeal community under thermophilic 
conditions in the early stage of HSAD (Fig. 7a) were Methanobrevibacter, 
Methanosarcina, Methanothermobacter, and Methanoculleus, which 
accounted for 18.8 %–48.7 %, 13.6 %–40.7 %, 10.9 %–55.8 %, and 3.3 
%–14.6 % of the total sequences, respectively, with RA > 5.0 %. As these 
dominant genera exhibit a heat tolerance ability, they can survive under 
thermophilic conditions and become dominant genera. Methano­
brevibacter and Methanothermobacter are hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogens that utilize H2 and CO2 to produce methane (de Barros et al., 
2017). Methanosarcina is the only methanogenic bacterium compatible 
with the acetate catabolic and hydrogenotrophic methanogenic path­
ways (Yan et al., 2022). Methanoculleus belongs to the group of acetic 
acid methanogens and can utilize acetic acid as a carbon and energy 
source to produce methane (Abid et al., 2021), demonstrating that 
hydrogen and methane yields are more effective under thermophilic 
conditions. Among them, T-Air and T-CO2 had the highest methane yield 
under thermophilic conditions, and the RA of Methanobrevibacter and 
Methanothermobacter in T-Air were higher than those in the control. The 
RA of Methanothermobacter in T-CO2 was VFAs and even higher at 55.8 
%, compared with only 10.9 % in the control. This result provided a 
basis for its high methane yield. Furthermore, Methanothermobacter was 
positively correlated with CMY and methane production rate (P < 0.05) 
(Fig. 8), as the activity of acetic acid trophic methanogens was inhibited 
with increasing ammonia concentration in the later stage of HSAD. 
Methanothermobacter, on the other hand, is a hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogen that exhibits a low sensitivity to ammonia and can perform 
methanogenesis at relatively high ammonia concentrations. Therefore, 
an increase in the RA of Methanothermobacter in the later stage of HSAD 
may lead to a concomitant increase in CMY. 
The dominant genera in the archaeal community under mesophilic 
conditions in the early stage of HSAD (Fig. 7a) were Methanobrevibacter, 
Methanosarcina, and Methanocorpusculum. Accounting for 40.6 %–68.3 
%, 11.9 %–47.4 %, and 3.2 %–37.9 % of the total sequences, respec­
tively, with RA > 5.0 %. Methanobrevibacter are hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens that utilize H2 and CO2 produced in the digestion system 
as substrates to produce methane (Cao et al., 2022). Compared with the 
DW, the experimental group with the addition of He-NBW and N2-NBW 
has a higher RA, which indicates that the addition of NBW exhibited a 
certain effect on methane yield. Methanosarcina is the only methano­

4. Conclusions 
In this study, we evaluated the changes in hydrolysis rate, digestion 
stability, methanogenic performance, and microbial community of 
HSAD by NBW with different gas species. T-Air, T-CO2, and M-Air were 
the most effective in high and mesophilic digesters. Compared with T 
and M, the TAN concentrations of T-Air, T-CO2, and M-Air were 
increased by 33.6%, 31.8%, and 34.7%, respectively, suggesting that T- 
Air, T-CO2, and M-Air may promote hydrolysis and hydrolyze the sub­
strate more thoroughly. Cumulative methane production of T-Air: 
227.09 mL g−1 VSadded, T-CO2: 226.12 mL g−1 VSadded increased by 
17.72 % and 17.22 % respectively compared to control T: 192.90 mL g−1 
VSadded, and M-Air: 162.39 mL g−1 VSadded increased by 9.68 % 
compared to control M: 148.05 mL g−1 VSadded. This indicates that NBW 
improved the methane production performance, and the increase in 
methane production also confirms the good stability of the system from 
the side. Also, the TVFAs/TA and FAN concentrations were smaller 
compared to T and M, indicating the improved stability of the system. 
Microbial community analysis revealed different increases in the RA of 
hydrolysis- and acid-producing bacteria such as Defluviitalea, Hal­
oplasma, and Bacillus at the genus level, as well as the RA of metha­
nogens such as Methanoculleus, Methanobrevibacter, and Methanosarcina 
had different degrees of increase. NBW of the remaining gases had a 
smaller effect but still had a positive effect compared with the control. 
The results showed that the addition of NBW promoted the hydrolysis of 
high-solids CM, enhanced the stability of the reaction, improved the 
methanogenic performance, and increased the RA of favorable genera. 
However, the mechanisms of the effects of NBW on HSAD were different 
for different gases, so the NBW-based HSAD system deserves further 
investigation.
